title: HashiCorp Vault: Secrets, Versions, and Policies
intro: Vault is a secrets store with three things a config file lacks: every read is authenticated and logged, access is granted by policy per path, and secrets have versions. You're on a workstation with the vault CLI pointed at the company Vault (VAULT_ADDR is set). The shop application's secrets live under secret/shop.

steps.prompt: Check the Vault server's state before anything else.
steps.fake_output:
Key             Value
---             -----
Seal Type       awskms
Initialized     true
Sealed          false
Version         1.17.2
Storage Type    raft
HA Enabled      true
HA Mode         active
steps.explanation: Initialised, unsealed, and this node is the active one in an HA cluster.
steps.why: 'Sealed' is the state that matters. Vault's data is encrypted on disk, and a sealed Vault holds no key to read it, so it serves nothing. It starts sealed after every restart. Here the seal type is awskms, meaning it unseals itself using a cloud key; with the default Shamir seal, several people must each enter a key share (identity-incident-002).

steps.prompt: Log in through the company identity provider.
steps.fake_output:
Complete the login via your OIDC provider. Launching browser to:
    https://auth.example.com/authorize?...

Success! You are now authenticated.
token_duration       8h
token_policies       ["default" "shop-dev"]
steps.explanation: You have a Vault token for 8 hours, carrying the policies default and shop-dev.
steps.why: Vault doesn't keep its own passwords for people: it trusts an identity provider and maps your groups to policies. Everything you do next is checked against those policies. The root token, created at initialisation, bypasses all of them; it should be revoked after setup and regenerated only for emergencies.

steps.fake_output:
====== Secret Path ======
secret/data/shop/database

======= Metadata =======
Key                Value
---                -----
created_time       2026-09-21T09:14:02Z
version            4

====== Data ======
Key         Value
---         -----
host        db.internal
password    s3cr3t-v4-example
username    shop_app
steps.explanation: Version 4 of the secret, created a week ago.
steps.why: Notice the real path is secret/data/shop/database. The key-value engine version 2 inserts 'data/' (and 'metadata/'), and policies must be written against those real paths, which is the usual reason a policy that looks right gives 'permission denied'. For scripts, 'vault kv get -field=password ...' prints just one value.

steps.prompt: Someone updated that secret last week and the app has had login failures since. Read the previous version, version 3.
steps.fake_output:
======= Metadata =======
Key                Value
---                -----
created_time       2026-06-02T14:40:11Z
version            3

====== Data ======
Key         Value
---         -----
host        db.internal
password    s3cr3t-v3-example
username    shop
steps.explanation: In version 3 the username was shop; version 4 changed it to shop_app.
steps.why: Versioning turns 'who changed the secret and what was it before?' into a lookup. 'vault kv rollback -version=3 secret/shop/database' would restore it as a new version. A secret in an environment file or a Kubernetes Secret has no history at all: an overwrite is final.

steps.prompt: Check what your token is allowed to do on the path secret/data/shop/database.
steps.explanation: Read only: you can't change or delete it.
steps.why: This answers 'why was I denied?' without guessing: it evaluates your token's policies for one path. Capabilities are create, read, update, delete, list, plus sudo and deny. Vault denies by default, so a path nobody granted is simply unreachable.

steps.prompt: The policy that grants that access is called shop-dev. Print it.
steps.explanation: Read on the shop secrets' data, and list on their metadata so you can browse the names.
steps.why: A policy is a list of paths and capabilities, in HCL. Least privilege here means one application gets read on its own subtree and nothing else, so a compromised app can't read another team's secrets. Policies are attached to identities (groups, Kubernetes service accounts), never to people one by one. Writing one is a Writing Lab (yaml-035).
